meta.title: Request Router
meta.subtitle: One endpoint, three execution paths: the router decides whether to answer **inline**, run a **lookup**, or start a **background job**.

tldr.headline: The router owns the decision; the client only sends a request.

points.title: One endpoint for every request
points.detail: Clients never pick a path, a worker, or a timeout. They send `POST /v1/ask` and read one response shape.

points.title: Classification happens once, up front
points.detail: A rule-based classifier picks the path; a model is consulted only when the rules are inconclusive.

points.title: Slow work never blocks the request
points.detail: Long-running work is queued and the client gets a `status_url` instead of waiting.

points.title: Every path converges on one envelope
points.detail: `{status, answer, links}` is returned whether the answer was inline, looked up, or deferred.

callouts.title: What the client sees
callouts.body: One endpoint and one response envelope. No path selection, no timeouts to tune, no knowledge of the search service or the job queue.

callouts.title: What the router absorbs
callouts.body: Classification, calling external services, deferring slow work, caching, and normalizing every result into the same envelope.

items.why: Most traffic matches simple rules. Calling a model for every request would add latency and cost for no gain; it is kept as a fallback for ambiguous input.

items.decision: Background jobs instead of long requests
items.why: Holding a connection open for 90 seconds breaks proxies and mobile clients. A `202` with a `status_url` is predictable and retry-safe.

items.decision: One response envelope for all paths
items.why: We considered per-path response types, but every client would then need three parsers. A shared envelope keeps client code path-agnostic.
